title: Superconducting Chip Claims: Don't Change Process Node, Change Temperature Zone—28nm Logic Can Hit 5nm Performance
dek: Move logic to liquid-helium temperatures and replace transistors with superconducting switches—that's Snowcap's bet: first tape out a RISC-V, then claim 28nm-class logic can deliver 5nm-class performance.
why: If you care about the compute power wall, this episode offers a third path—not squeezing transistors, but moving the entire logic to liquid-helium temperatures; a former Intel CEO has placed his bet. The risks and numbers are laid out, worth a listen.
who: Hard-tech investors who want to verify whether superconducting computing is a real path or just a story, and CPU/supercomputer architects studying the chip power wall.
skip: If you're familiar with overclocking and liquid-nitrogen cooling, you can skip the overclocking preamble from 0:00 to 2:01.

points.h: Extreme overclocking's ceiling is cooling, not the chip
points.body: The episode opens with the overclocking industry: everyday chips rely on air cooling, higher-power ones use water cooling, and beyond that you need dry ice, liquid nitrogen, and other sub-zero media. Extreme overclockers push voltage to chase maximum frequencies, making chips hotter, so they must cool them in increasingly extreme ways. The host says he was once an extreme overclocker and even took second place in the world—though it lasted only a day and a half. His key reference: such overclocking is only for running benchmark tests at 8.5GHz for a few minutes, whereas true superconducting computing aims not for instantaneous records but for logic that operates at near-zero power.

points.h: Liquid-helium overclocking's real cost is the transfer tube, not the helium
points.body: Going from liquid nitrogen to liquid helium, physics starts to interfere. Liquid helium costs about 20 times as much as liquid nitrogen (which is about $1 per liter), but that's not the main expense: the transfer tube that moves liquid helium from a large storage tank into a 3-4 kg copper overclocking pot costs $5,000 per use. Intel and Asus have both done liquid-helium overclocking, with records already surpassing 9GHz. The host warns that material behavior changes dramatically at such temperatures—some platforms have a 'cold bug' where the system simply won't boot once it gets too cold; only platforms without the cold bug are suitable for liquid-helium play.

points.h: Superconductivity's allure isn't speed, it's zero resistance
points.body: Overclocking is about squeezing frequency out of existing materials; superconductivity is another narrative: electrons flow through superconducting materials with no resistance, meaning free transport. Currently, most superconductors require extremely low temperatures, and room-temperature superconductivity remains in a state of repeated research setbacks. The key extrapolation here: if the entire chip's switching logic could operate in a superconducting state, per-operation energy would be 'several orders of magnitude' better than current laptops. The host deliberately speaks boldly but then pulls back—superconductivity is still the holy grail, not yet achieved. This sets the stage for Snowcap's entry.

points.h: Former Intel CEO bets on temperature zone, not process node
points.body: Snowcap Compute has just completed its seed round, and its board includes former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger. Their bet is on building superconducting chips that operate at about 4-15K, i.e., liquid-helium temperatures. Structurally, it's no longer billions of transistors but a new type of switch that works at superconducting temperatures—the Josephson junction. For now, Snowcap's goal is to first build a RISC-V-class CPU at low temperatures, making power consumption nearly free; the trade-off is that the entire machine must stay in the liquid-helium temperature range, and cooling itself consumes energy.

points.h: Superconducting logic's new variable: compatibility with standard EDA flows
points.body: Long-term researchers are not scarce: US defense contractors have made chips integrating tens of millions of Josephson junctions, and IMEC has reached hundreds of millions, also building supporting logic and EDA tools. Snowcap's differentiator is compatibility: they say this superconducting logic can fit into standard EDA flows and can be taped out on ordinary CMOS processes, using niobium titanium nitride as the material. The core conclusion the host heard: the energy-efficiency advantage from superconductivity is equivalent to achieving near-5nm chip performance with 28nm logic—note this isn't a smaller process node, but an equivalent gain from lower power.

points.h: Cryo CMOS is just an intermediate state; the real hurdle is scale
points.body: Snowcap plans to deliver its first chip in 2026, followed by a deployable RISC-V design. The intermediate state can be seen in cryo CMOS: it operates in the liquid-nitrogen temperature range of about 72-77K, and while it isn't superconducting, the low temperature itself reduces power. The real hurdle is crossing from cryo CMOS into superconductivity; the host's skepticism is 'can you scale up performance at high levels'—being able to run and being able to commercialize at scale are two different things.

points.h: Low-temperature startup isn't rare; the hard part is keeping the whole machine in liquid helium
points.body: This section provides a real-world footnote on low-temperature tape-outs: AMD's first Zen 1 A0 sample, which leaked when AMD was most cash-strapped, could only boot at sub-zero temperatures on dry ice due to a design flaw, and was later fixed to run at room temperature. This shows that low temperatures in testing and startup aren't unusual; but keeping an entire processor in the liquid-helium temperature range involves infrastructure issues, including helium supply—liquid helium is also the lifeblood of MRI machines' superconducting magnets, and there was a helium shortage a few years ago.

points.h: Snowcap isn't selling IP; it's selling a closed appliance
points.body: Snowcap positions itself not as an IP seller but as delivering complete systems. The host's judgment: precisely because of the infrastructure barrier of the liquid-helium temperature range, the product will be nearly a closed appliance, and the software stack will need to be rebuilt. A seed-stage company still has Series A/B/C rounds to get through; however, they've already brought in advisors and former employees from Apple, Nvidia, and Google. On this topic, it's worth staying skeptical and also worth following.
